explanation:
## The program

```cpp
int gcd(int a, int b)
{
    while (b != 0)
    {
        int r{ a % b };
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

long long lcm(int a, int b)
{
    return static_cast<long long>(a / gcd(a, b)) * b;
}
```

## Why Euclid works

Any number dividing both `a` and `b` also divides `a % b`, because
`a % b` is `a` minus a whole number of `b`s. So the pair `(a, b)`
and the pair `(b, a % b)` have exactly the same set of common
divisors — and therefore the same greatest one. The second pair is
strictly smaller, so repeating it must stop, and it stops when the
second number is 0, at which point the first is the answer.

It is fast: the remainder at least halves every two steps, so the
number of passes is proportional to the number of *digits* rather
than to the numbers themselves. `gcd(99999, 100000)` takes three.

The three-line swap is the whole loop body. Writing it without the
temporary — `b = a % b; a = ...` — does not work, because the old
`a` is needed twice.

## lcm does not deserve an algorithm

For positive `a` and `b`:

```
gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) = a × b
```

so the lcm is `a * b / gcd(a, b)`, and the function is one line.
Writing a second search loop for it would be slower, longer, and a
second place for the same kind of bug.

Reaching for a function you have already written is the whole of
"decomposition" at this scale. It is not an architectural principle;
it is noticing that the thing in front of you is made of a thing you
have.

## Divide first

```cpp
a * b / gcd(a, b)             // 99999 * 100000 overflows an int
a / gcd(a, b) * b             // 99999 / 1 * 100000 — fine
```

Integer division normally loses information, so "divide last" is a
reasonable default habit. This is the exception, and it is exact: by
definition `gcd(a, b)` divides `a` with no remainder, so dividing
early throws nothing away. Having established that, doing it first
keeps the intermediate value small.

The `static_cast<long long>` then goes on the *left* operand before
the multiply, so the multiplication itself is done in 64 bits.
Casting the result instead — `static_cast<long long>(a / g * b)` —
would be too late, exactly as with the mean and the `double`.

## What this does not check

Zero and negative inputs, which the constraints exclude.
`gcd(0, 0)` has no sensible answer and this loop returns 0;
`lcm` would then divide by it. `std::gcd` and `std::lcm` in
`<numeric>` handle the signs and are what you would reach for in
real code — writing Euclid by hand once is the point here.
